lines.text: Rahul's placement bot goes live, and a few thousand students show up. Every question now costs tokens and seconds.
The bill is simple: input tokens times the input price, plus output tokens times the output price.
So measure first. Every response reports its own usage, so log tokens, seconds and cost for each request.
Lever one: send fewer tokens. Trim the system prompt, retrieve four chunks instead of ten, and cap the output.
Lever two: route. An easy question goes to a small model, and a hard one goes to the large one.
Then rerun your eval set, because a cheaper wrong answer isn't cheaper.
Lever three is the best one: a cache. Many students ask exactly the same question.
Answer it once and store it. Every repeat is a cache hit that skips the model: no tokens, almost no wait.
Careful when you match paraphrases. A TCS question and an Infosys question look almost identical, but need different answers.
For speed, don't trust the average. One slow request in twenty hides inside it.
Report p ninety-five instead: the time that ninety-five percent of requests beat.
So the order is: measure, then cache, route and trim. The cheapest request is the one that never reaches the model.
Next lesson: your portfolio, resume and interviews.
